content: Therapeutic and surgical services should be integrated and provided in conjunction with services for individuals affected by other neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), diabetes, and non-leprosy-related disabilities. In Paraguay, since 2000, the leprosy program has ensured the presence of a dedicated focal person in all 18 health regions to assess and manage disabilities and leprosy reactions. These public health workers, funded by the government and supported by additional resources from the German Tuberculosis and Leprosy Relief Association (GLRA), conduct field trips within their regions. They also receive technical advice from Hospital Mennonita Km 81 for managing complex cases. These health workers ensure proper disability grading at diagnosis and upon completion of multidrug therapy (MDT). They promptly examine patients for reactions and are skilled in administering corticosteroid-based anti-inflammatory treatments. Additionally, they provide tools to patients with insensitive hands and feet to prevent further impairments. Reconstructive surgery can be delivered through surgical camps, which are effective in reaching leprosy-affected individuals in remote or vulnerable areas. Leprosy management often requires lifelong care, as new disabilities can arise during treatment or later due to reactions or irreversible nerve damage. Identifying individuals at risk of further disabilities at the end of MDT and continuing surveillance of their disability status is crucial. It is also essential to determine the number of leprosy-affected individuals requiring self-care training, disability management, or rehabilitation to plan post-MDT care effectively. National programs should incorporate mechanisms to capture this information, as current surveillance systems do not. Proposed actions include establishing systems to record and report individuals with existing disabilities and those at risk of leprosy-related disabilities post-MDT. Patients at risk should be offered semi-active surveillance to prevent social exclusion due to worsening impairments. Encouraging patients with sensory impairments to join self-care groups can help prevent secondary impairments. Care for individuals with Grade 2 Disability (G2D) should be ensured through public-private partnerships, focusing on disability prevention, wound care, protective footwear, self-management devices, and reconstructive surgery. In high-burden settings, referral centers for leprosy disability care and reconstructive surgery should be linked with social and welfare services to ensure accessibility. Self-care and community self-care groups should be integrated into national leprosy guidelines, and their activities supported. Public-private partnerships should be established to ensure service coverage and supervise non-governmental facilities for compliance with national agreements and quality standards. In low-burden settings, access to at least one specialized disability care center should be ensured. Integrated services for leprosy, other NTDs, and non-communicable disease-related disabilities should be promoted to cover services like wound care and reconstructive surgery. Coordination with social and welfare schemes should ensure free access to specialized care for leprosy-affected individuals. Strengthening surveillance for antimicrobial resistance is critical. While the current MDT treatment recommended by WHO is effective, the emergence of rifampicin, dapsone, and ofloxacin resistance has been reported with the advent of DNA sequencing methods. The Global Leprosy Programme (GLP), in collaboration with TNF, initiated a global drug resistance surveillance network in 2009, supported by ILEP members since 2011. Although drug resistance is not yet a significant issue, robust surveillance systems are needed to monitor trends and develop effective countermeasures. Improved reporting of relapses, enhanced testing among new cases, and standardized case definitions are necessary. PCR testing should be available at least at the national level for MB cases, and a system for dispatching samples to specialized molecular centers or international reference laboratories should be established. In India, The Leprosy Mission Trust India (TLMTI), in collaboration with ILEP members, coordinates with the government to facilitate reconstructive surgeries for leprosy-affected individuals. TLMTI operates 13 hospitals across eight states, recognized by the government for leprosy-related reconstructive surgeries. Over the past decade, 1,100 to 1,300 surgeries have been performed annually in these hospitals. TLMTI surgeons have also operated in government hospitals in states like Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Sikkim, Assam, and Meghalaya, training local surgeons in leprosy-related reconstructive procedures. Promoting innovative approaches for training, referrals, and sustaining expertise in leprosy is essential, especially as leprosy becomes a rare disease. Technological advancements, such as mobile phones, social media, and internet access, offer opportunities for long-distance training and teleconsultations. However, the quality of online training must be certified, and care quality monitored at the service delivery level. Training needs should be assessed and tailored to the country’s health system. The GLP, in collaboration with ILEP, has established a surveillance network to collect global data on MDT resistance. This network meets biannually to review results and plan future work. Preventive tools for leprosy infection and disease among already infected individuals could significantly impact leprosy elimination. While no vaccine has shown high efficacy, single-dose rifampicin (SDR) chemoprophylaxis offers partial protection with negligible side effects and drug-resistance risks. Combined immunoand chemoprophylaxis appear more effective among leprosy case contacts. However, evidence on the feasibility of using such tools at the country level remains limited. Diagnostic tests for infection detection would enable better targeting of preventive measures, but no experimental tests have been approved for routine use.
